title: How to become a coach
summary: A good shooter is not yet a coach. How to find coach training, why qualifications differ between countries, and what a coach needs beyond technique.

body.html: Many shooters one day wonder whether they should start teaching others. It is a fine goal, but shooting well and teaching well are different skills. A coach explains things simply, spots a fault from the outside and picks an exercise for this particular person.

Coaching qualifications differ between countries. In some, the national federation runs coach courses with several levels (level 1, level 2 and so on). In others it is a shooting association or a sports school. Paid coaching may need an official document, insurance or a permit. So start by finding out the rules in your country.

Coach training usually starts with safety on the ground and the gun itself. Then come gun fit (adjusting the gun so it shoots where you look) and finding the master eye (the eye that takes the lead when you aim). Courses also cover the basics of technique and working with beginners and children. They often end with a practical assessment.
Safety comes first. A coach is responsible for more than technique. The student must handle the gun correctly, wear glasses and hearing protection, and know the local laws on guns and cartridges.

A useful path is to work alongside an experienced coach: help at sessions, watch and ask questions. You learn what books do not teach, such as calming a nervous student or explaining one thing in three different ways.

In both Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting, coaching a shooter (giving them advice) is not allowed during a competition. The shooter gets a yellow card (a formal warning), and the referee sends the person giving the advice out of the shooting area. A coach works before and after the competition.
Once you are a coach, the ClayArena coaches directory can help students find you. It shows who you are and which disciplines you teach: Finding a coach and a shooting ground on ClayArena.
The Academy route for new coaches helps you prepare, but it is not a coaching qualification.

key_points.html: Shooting well and teaching well are different skills.
Coaching qualifications depend on the country: find out the local rules.
Coach training covers safety, gun fit, the master eye and working with beginners.
Coaching a shooter during a competition is not allowed in either discipline.
Working alongside an experienced coach teaches a lot.

did_you_know.html: The rule is about the advice, not the job title. A tip from a friend or a parent during the competition can also count as coaching.

quiz.q: Are coaching qualifications the same in all countries?

options.text: Yes, FITASC issues all of them
No, they depend on the country
There are no qualifications at all

quiz.explain: Coach training and the rules for coaches differ from country to country.

quiz.q: What happens if someone coaches a shooter during a competition?

options.text: Yellow card for the shooter; the coach is sent out
Nothing, as long as it is a coach
The shooter is given an extra target

quiz.explain: Coaching during a competition is not allowed in Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting.

quiz.q: What comes first for a coach?
quiz.explain: Safety comes before technique and before everything else.
